title: Raymond Scott, Lou Shuby, Johnny Williams and New York studio players
summary: Talk of Wade Schlegel's brother with Raymond Scott in California, bassist Lou Shuby, drummer Johnny Williams, and Hirsch's own work with Studebaker transcriptions and sitting in at NBC while in the Navy.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working with Sinatra: bands, Vegas and the Sands

blocks.x: Raymond Scott. Raymond Scott. He was with Raymond Scott. Raymond Scott. They were in California under contract to the studio that did The Little Dancer. The little gal. She was famous. and they were out there about 1937. They were there for two years. In fact, they had Shuby, Lou Shuby was the bass player. I don't know if you know Lou Shuby. Lou Shuby was a contractor at CBS. He took a leave of absence for two years. He had a drummer by the name of Johnny Williams. Johnny Williams, who I've heard from since, is Johnny Williams, who is the father of John Williams. Really? Inducted.

Yeah. I used Johnny when I had charge of the Studebaker transcriptions. When him was in San Francisco, I came back to New York and had charge of the... I had the guy that wrote Tenderly and played piano. I had... I didn't have an author. I had Chris Griffin, who was with Goodman. And I don't remember the whole gang of it. These guys were fantastic musicians. Ray Block was a conductor. It sounds silly, but I mean, it's all true. And I enjoyed these things. And I worked with a lot of great musicians. And being in New York, I got to know them all. In fact, Sammy Weiss, who was Jack Benny's drummer until he died, was Phil Harris' band. I used to go over to NBC when I was in the Navy, and I'd say, man, go upstairs and play with so-and-so. I mean, Paul Lavelle. Paul Lavelle. He's conducting a symphony orchestra, and he needs somebody to play vibes, and I don't know how to play vibes. He says, go ahead and substitute for me. I'd go up there with a sailor suit on and substitute for him with Paul Lavelle in the orchestra. But Sid Weiss was a good friend of mine. Sid Weiss. And so was Phil Harris, a very dear friend. Phil Harris had paid me the greatest compliment in the world
